title: Prince Yūsuf ibn Saʿd leaves the settling of Ishbīliya and turns to promoting Andalusī culture
Yūsuf ibn Ismāʿīl, lord of the Ṭāʾifa of Banbalūna since 1411, dies of a camp fever at fifty-six. His son Aḥmad, once of the dīwān and one of the ablest men of the house, succeeds him

data.account: War rages in France again (Trent); the sides aren't in the account

title: The Emperor's spies travel north to the three kingdoms, proclaiming to every Iberian the return of al-Andalus, while the casus belli for the next war is prepared

data.account: our spies travel north to the three remaining Kingdoms ... proclaiming the return of Al-Andalus to all Iberians as our casus belli is prepared (Trent)

title: The Emperor begins a great expansion of the army: armouries are built in a dozen towns and cities across the empire, so that each can raise men of its own

data.buildings: armouries in about a dozen towns and cities
data.inSave: armouries at Orihuela, Évora, Lisbon, Santarém, Toledo, Córdoba, Écija, Almería, Granada and Málaga (save of 25 May 1428)

title: In preparation for the war a Jamāʿa is called, and with it another chance to take a privilege from the umarāʾ: the Primacy of Nobility, by which the great houses count themselves the Emperor's equals and must be consulted before every important decision

data.text: The Nobility of our country has proven to be key allies, as they support most of our enterprises and are the backbone of our armies. For this reason, they consider themselves our equals, and they have become so crucial to the government that we must consult with them before making important decisions (the game's text)

effects.modifiers: political influence gain −15%, discipline +5%, monthly progress to aristocracy +0.10

data.outcome: revoked (the privilege is gone in the save of 25 May 1428)

title: The Primacy of Nobility, held by the umarāʾ since the founding of the realm, is revoked. The great houses no longer count themselves the Emperor's equals or must be consulted on his decisions. Their content falls to about one in six, and the realm's peace to almost nothing

data.jamaa: called 25 May 1428; the nobles' agenda is to remove the burghers' mansions, the ʿulamāʾ's a change of policy

title: By 1428 Ishbīliya has the Andalusī madrasa, a great school of the empire's own (nd_adu_madrasa, a building of the Al-Andalus formation)

At the Emperor's insistence, and to answer the anger of the umarāʾ, a great campaign of rural renewal begins: in nearly every large village of the empire a granary is built, a safe communal store where farming settlements can set aside part of each harvest. The Emperor remembers how lean and dear bread could be in the hard years of the wars with Qashtāla

data.buildings: village granaries in nearly every major village
data.purpose: to counter the nobility's mass frustration; safe communal stores for part of each harvest (Trent)
data.memory: how lean and expensive food could get during the leaner years against the Castilians (Trent)

title: Wheat farms, windmills and acequias are built across several rural regions to fill the new granaries, and lumber mills to build them and, in time, renew them, all at very little cost to the umarāʾ or the peasants

data.cost: very low cost to the nobility and peasantry (Trent)

title: Andalusī envoys sail the new sea roads and travel inland to Niani, the city of Mansa Tiramakhan of Mālī. The two empires exchange gifts, and the Mansa exempts Andalusī traders from tariffs throughout his empire. Expeditions are already being planned to bring the gold of Mālī north, to the jewellers of al-Andalus and for resale to the Europeans

data.route: by the new naval routes, then inland (Trent)
data.result: Andalusī traders exempt from tariffs in the Mali Empire (Trent)
data.plans: expeditions to bring Mali's gold north for the Andalusī jewellery market and for resale to Europe (Trent)
data.mali: 14th in the world, 82 towns and 92 in subjects; Mansa Tiramakhan since 1410, heir Majan born 1405 (world file of 25 May 1428)
